Stalin believed in an inevitable "class war" between the world's proletariat and bourgeoisie[590] in which the working classes would prove victorious and establish a dictatorship of the proletariat,[591] regarding the Soviet Union as an example of such a state.[592] He also believed that this proletarian state would need to introduce repressive measures against foreign and domestic "enemies" to ensure the full crushing of the propertied classes,[593] and thus the class war would intensify with the advance of socialism.[594] As a propaganda tool, the shaming of "enemies" explained all inadequate economic and political outcomes, the hardships endured by the populace, and military failures.[595]

Stalin adhered to the Leninist variant of Marxism.[596] In his book, Foundations of Leninism, he stated that "Leninism is the Marxism of the epoch of imperialism and of the proletarian revolution".[597] He claimed to be a loyal Leninist,[598] although was—according to Service—"not a blindly obedient Leninist".[599] Stalin respected Lenin, but not uncritically,[600] and spoke out when he believed that Lenin was wrong.[599] During the period of his revolutionary activity, Stalin regarded some of Lenin's views and actions as being the self-indulgent activities of a spoilt émigré, deeming them counterproductive for those Bolshevik activists based within the Russian Empire itself.[601] After the October Revolution, they continued to have differences,[602] although Kotkin suggested that Stalin's friendship with Lenin was "the single most important relationship in Stalin's life".[603]

Stalin viewed nations as contingent entities which were formed by capitalism and could merge into others.[604] Ultimately, he believed that all nations would merge into a single, global community,[604] and regarded all nations as inherently equal.[605] In his work, he stated that "the right of secession" should be offered to the ethnic minorities of the Russian Empire, but that they should not be encouraged to take that option.[606] He was of the view that if they became fully autonomous, then they would end up being controlled by the most reactionary elements of their community.[606] Stalin's push for Soviet westward expansion into Eastern Europe resulted in accusations of Russian imperialism.[607]

Personal life and characteristics

Ethnically Georgian,[608] Stalin grew up speaking the Georgian language,[609] and did not begin learning Russian until age eight or nine.[610] It has been argued that his ancestry was genetically Ossetian, but he never acknowledged an Ossetian identity.[611] He remained proud of his Georgian identity,[612] and throughout his life retained a heavy Georgian accent when speaking Russian.[613][614] Some colleagues described him as "Asiatic", and he supposedly said that "I am not a European man, but an Asian, a Russified Georgian".[615]

Described as soft-spoken[616] and a poor orator,[617] Stalin's style was "simple and clear, without flights of fancy, catchy phrases or platform histrionics".[618] He rarely spoke before large audiences and preferred to express himself in writing.[619] In adulthood, Stalin measured 1.70 m (5 feet 7 inches) in height.[620][621] His moustached face was pock-marked from smallpox during childhood; this was airbrushed from published photographs.[622] His left arm had been injured in childhood leaving it shorter than his right and lacking in flexibility.[623] Stalin was a lifelong smoker, who smoked both a pipe and cigarettes.[624] Publicly, he lived relatively plainly, with simple and inexpensive clothing and furniture.[625] As leader, Stalin rarely left Moscow unless for holiday;[626] he disliked travel,[627] and refused to travel by plane.[628] In 1934, his Kuntsevo Dacha was built 9 km (5.6 mi) from the Kremlin and became his primary residence.[629] He holidayed in the south USSR every year from 1925 to 1936 and 1945 to 1951,[630] often in Abkhazia, being a friend of its leader, Nestor Lakoba.[631]

Personality

Trotsky and several other Soviet figures promoted the idea that Stalin was a mediocrity,[632] a characterisation which gained widespread acceptance outside of the Soviet Union during his lifetime.[633] However, historians have described him as having a complex mind,[634] remarkable self-control,[635] and strong memory.[636] Stalin was a diligent worker[637] and an effective and strategic organiser,[638] with a keen interest in learning.[639] As a leader, he meticulously scrutinised details, from film scripts to military plans,[640] and judged others by their inner strength and cleverness.[641] He was skilled at playing different roles depending on the audience,[642] as well as in deception.[643] Although he could be rude,[644] Stalin rarely raised his voice;[645] however, as his health deteriorated, he became unpredictable and bad-tempered.[646] He could be charming and enjoyed cracking jokes when relaxed.[639] At social events, Stalin encouraged singing and drinking, hoping others would drunkenly reveal secrets to him.[647]

Stalin lacked compassion,[648] possibly exacerbated by his repeated imprisonments and exiles,[649] though he occasionally showed kindness to strangers, even during the Great Purge.[650] He could be self-righteous,[651] resentful,[652] and vindictive,[653] often holding grudges for years.[654] By the 1920s, he had become suspicious and conspiratorial, prone to believing in plots against him and international conspiracies.[655] While he never attended torture sessions or executions,[656] Stalin took pleasure in degrading and humiliating people and kept even close associates in a state of "unrelieved fear".[607] Service suggested he had tendencies toward a paranoid and sociopathic personality disorder.[634] Historian E. A. Rees believed it was psychopathy that bred Stalin's tyranny, citing a 1927 diagnosis by neuropathologist Vladimir Bekhterev that described him as a "typical case of severe paranoia".[657] Others have linked Stalin's brutality to his commitment to the survival of the Soviet Union and Marxist–Leninist ideology.[658]

Stalin had a keen interest in the arts.[659] He protected certain Soviet writers, such as Mikhail Bulgakov, even when their work was criticised as harmful to his government.[660] Stalin enjoyed classical music,[661] owned around 2,700 records,[662] and often attended the Bolshoi Theatre in the 1930s and 40s.[663] His taste was conservative, favouring classical drama, opera, and ballet over what he dismissed as experimental "formalism",[610] and disliked avant-garde in the visual arts.[664] An autodidact,[665] Stalin was a voracious reader who kept over 20,000 books,[666] with little fiction.[667] His favourite subject was history, and he was especially interested in the reigns of Russian leaders Ivan the Terrible, Peter the Great, and Catherine the Great.[668] Lenin was his favourite author, but he read and appreciated works by Trotsky and other adversaries.[668]

Relationships and family

Stalin married his first wife, Ekaterina Svanidze, in 1906. Volkogonov suggested that she was "probably the one human being he had really loved".[669] When she died in 1907, Stalin allegedly said: "This creature softened my heart of stone. She died and with her died my last warm feelings for humanity."[670] They had a son, Yakov, who frequently frustrated and annoyed Stalin.[671] After Yakov was captured by the German Army during World War II, Stalin refused to agree to a prisoner exchange between him and German field marshal Friedrich Paulus, and Yakov died at a Nazi concentration camp in 1943.[672]

In exile in Solvychegodsk in 1910, Stalin had an affair with his landlady, Maria Kuzakova, who in 1911 gave birth to his alleged second son, Konstantin Kuzakov,[673] who later taught philosophy at the Leningrad Military Mechanical Institute, but never met Stalin.[674] In 1914 in Kureika, Stalin, aged 35, had a relationship with Lidia Pereprygina, aged 14 (considered a minor at the time), who allegedly became pregnant with Stalin's child.[675][676] In December 1914, Pereprygina gave birth to the child, although the infant died soon after.[677] In 1916, Pereprygina was pregnant again. She gave birth to their alleged son, Alexander Davydov, in around April 1917. He was raised as the son of a peasant fisherman;[678] Stalin later came to know of the child's existence but showed no interest in him.[679]

Stalin had a difficult relationship with his second wife, Nadezhda Alliluyeva, whom he married in 1919, as they often fought.[680] They had two biological children—a son, Vasily, and daughter, Svetlana—and adopted another son, Artyom Sergeev, in 1921.[681] Though it is unclear if Stalin had a mistress during or after this marriage,[682] she suspected he was unfaithful,[683] and committed suicide in 1932.[684] Stalin regarded Vasily as spoiled and often chastised his behaviour; as Stalin's son, he was swiftly promoted through the Red Army and allowed a lavish lifestyle.[685] Conversely, Stalin had an affectionate relationship with Svetlana during her childhood,[686] and was very fond of Artyom.[681] He disapproved of Svetlana's suitors and husbands, which put strain on their relationship.[687] After World War II, he made little time for his children, and his family played a diminishing role in his life.[688] After Stalin's death, Svetlana changed her surname to Alliluyeva,[578] and defected to the US.[689]

Legacy

Leninists remain divided in their views on Stalin; some view him as Lenin's authentic successor, while others believe he betrayed Lenin's ideas by deviating from them.[607] The historian Robert Conquest stated that Stalin perhaps "determined the course of the twentieth century" more than any other individual.[690] For most Westerners and anti-communist Russians, he is viewed overwhelmingly negatively as a mass murderer;[691] for significant numbers of Russians and Georgians, he is regarded as a great statesman and state-builder.[691] The historian Dmitri Volkogonov characterised him as "one of the most powerful figures in human history."[692]

According to Service, Stalin strengthened and stabilised the Soviet Union.[693] In under three decades, Stalin transformed the country into a major industrial world power,[694] one which could "claim impressive achievements" in terms of urbanisation, military strength, education and Soviet pride.[695] Under his rule, the average Soviet life expectancy grew due to improved living conditions, nutrition and medical care[696] as mortality rates declined.[697] Although millions of Soviet citizens despised him, support for Stalin was nevertheless widespread throughout Soviet society.[695] Conversely, the historian Vadim Rogovin argued that Stalin's purges "caused losses to the communist movement both in the USSR and throughout the world from which the movement has not recovered to this very day".[698] Similarly, Nikita Khrushchev believed his purges of the Old Bolsheviks and leading figures in the military and academia had "undoubtedly" weakened the nation.[699]

Stalin's necessity for the Soviet Union's economic development has been questioned, and it has been argued that his policies from 1928 onwards may have been a limiting factor.[700] Stalin's Soviet Union has been characterised as a totalitarian state,[701] with Stalin its authoritarian leader.[702] Various biographers have described him as a dictator,[703] an autocrat,[704] or accused him of practising Caesarism.[705] Montefiore argued that while Stalin initially ruled as part of a Communist Party oligarchy, the government transformed into a personal dictatorship in 1934,[706] with Stalin only becoming "absolute dictator" after March–June 1937, when senior military and NKVD figures were eliminated.[707] In both the Soviet Union and elsewhere he came to be portrayed as an "Oriental despot".[708] McDermott nevertheless cautioned against "over-simplistic stereotypes"—promoted in the fiction of writers like Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn—which portrayed Stalin as an omnipotent and omnipresent tyrant who controlled every aspect of Soviet life.[709]

A vast literature devoted to Stalin has been produced.[710] During Stalin's lifetime, his approved biographies were largely hagiographic in content.[711] Stalin ensured that these works gave very little attention to his early life, particularly because he did not wish to emphasise his Georgian origins in a state numerically dominated by Russians.[712] Since his death many more biographies have been written,[713] although until the 1980s these relied largely on the same sources of information.[713] Under Mikhail Gorbachev's Soviet administration various previously classified files on Stalin's life were made available to historians,[713] at which point he became "one of the most urgent and vital issues on the public agenda" in the Soviet Union.[714] After the dissolution of the Union in 1991, the rest of the archives were opened to historians, resulting in much new information about Stalin coming to light,[715] and producing a flood of new research.[710]

Death toll

Main article: Excess mortality in the Soviet Union under Joseph Stalin

Before the dissolution of the Soviet Union and the archival revelations, some Western historians estimated that the numbers killed by Stalin's regime were 20 million or higher.[716][717][718][719] The scholarly consensus affirms that Soviet archival materials declassified in 1991 contain irrefutable data much lower than Western sources used prior to 1991, such as statements from emigres and other informants.[720] Based on these records, scholars have estimated that 1.8 million people were deported to remote regions of the country during Stalin's dekulakisation campaign, in addition to 1 million peasants and ethnic minorities deported in the 1930s, and 3.5 million people (mainly ethnic minorities) deported in the 1940s and 1950s, for a total of 6.3 million.[721] The Soviet archives also contain official records of 799,455 executions from 1921 to 1953,[722][723] around 1.5 to 1.7 million deaths in Gulag camps (out of an estimated 18 million people who passed through),[724][725][726] some 390,000[727] deaths during the dekulakisation forced resettlement, and up to 400,000 deaths of persons deported during the 1940s,[728] with a total of about 3.3 million officially recorded victims in these categories.[729] According to historian Stephen Wheatcroft, approximately 1 million of these deaths were "purposive" while the rest happened through neglect and irresponsibility.[730]

The deaths of at least 3.5 to 6.5 million[731] persons in the Soviet famine of 1932–1933 are sometimes, though not always, included with the victims of the Stalin era.[730] Stalin has also been accused of genocide in the cases of forced population transfer of ethnic minorities across the Soviet Union and the Holodomor famine.[732] However, British historian Michael Ellman argues that mass deaths from famines should be placed in a different category than the repression victims, mentioning that throughout Russian history famines and droughts have been a common occurrence.[733] Famines were widespread throughout the world in the 19th and 20th centuries in countries such as China, India, Ireland, and Russia.[734] Ellman compared the behaviour of the Stalinist regime to that of the British government (towards Ireland and India) and the G8 in contemporary times, and Stalin's "behaviour was no worse than that of many rulers in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries".[734]

In the Soviet Union and post-Soviet states

See also: Neo-Stalinism and Nostalgia for the Soviet Union

Shortly after his death, the Soviet Union went through a period of de-Stalinisation. Malenkov denounced the Stalin personality cult,[735] and the cult was subsequently criticised in Pravda.[736] In 1956, Khrushchev gave his "Secret Speech", titled "On the Cult of Personality and Its Consequences", to a closed session of the Party's 20th Congress. There, Khrushchev denounced Stalin for both his mass repression and his personality cult.[737] He repeated these denunciations at the 22nd Party Congress in October 1962.[738] In October 1961, Stalin's body was removed from the mausoleum and buried in the Kremlin Wall Necropolis, the location marked by a bust.[739] Stalingrad was renamed Volgograd that year.[740]

Khrushchev's de-Stalinisation process ended when he was replaced as leader by Leonid Brezhnev in 1964; the latter introduced a level of re-Stalinisation within the Soviet Union.[741] In 1969 and again in 1979, plans were proposed for a full rehabilitation of Stalin's legacy but on both occasions were halted due to fears of damaging the USSR's public image.[742] Mikhail Gorbachev saw the total denunciation of Stalin as necessary for the regeneration of Soviet society.[743]

After the fall of the Soviet Union in 1991, Boris Yeltsin continued Gorbachev's denunciation of Stalin but added to it a denunciation of Lenin.[743] His successor Vladimir Putin did not seek to rehabilitate Stalin but emphasised the celebration of Soviet achievements under Stalin's leadership rather than the Stalinist repressions.[744] In October 2017, Putin opened the Wall of Grief, a memorial to the victims of Stalin's repressions, in Moscow.[745] Following the 2022 Russian invasion of Ukraine, the government and general public of Russia has been accused of rehabilitating Stalin.[746] In May 2025, Russian authorities re-added a statue of Stalin at the Taganskaya metro station after the original was removed in 1966 as part of the 90th anniversary of the opening of the metro.[747][748] In July, the Communist Party of the Russian Federation described Khrushchev's 1956 speech denouncing Stalin's cult of personality as a "mistake" and "politically biased", further urging Putin to restore "Stalingrad" as the official name of the Russian city of Volgograd.[749]

Admiration for Stalin has remained consistently widespread in Georgia, although Georgian attitudes have been very divided.[750] A number of Georgians resent criticism of Stalin, the most famous figure from their nation's modern history.[751]

  1. ^ The office of General Secretary was abolished in 1952, but Stalin continued to exercise its powers as the highest-ranking member of the party Secretariat.
  2. ^ Before 1946, the title of the office was People's Commissar for Defence, and briefly People's Commissar for the Armed Forces.
  3. ^ Founded as the RSDLP(b) in 1912; renamed the RCP(b) in 1918, AUCP(b) in 1925, and CPSU in 1952.
  4. ^ While forced to give up control of the Secretariat almost immediately after succeeding Stalin as the body's de facto head, Malenkov was still recognised as "first among equals" within the regime for over a year. As late as March 1954, he remained listed as first in the Soviet leadership and continued to chair meetings of the Politburo.
  5. ^ In this name that follows East Slavic naming customs, the patronymic is Vissarionovich and the family name is Stalin.
  6. ^ /ˈstɑːlɪn/;[1] Russian: Иосиф Виссарионович Сталин, romanized: Iosif Vissarionovich Stalin [ɪˈosʲɪf vʲɪssərʲɪˈonəvʲɪtɕ ˈstalʲɪn] ⓘ; Georgian: იოსებ ბესარიონის ძე სტალინი, romanized: ioseb besarionis dze st'alini
  7. ^ a b Stalin's birth name was Ioseb Besarionis dze Jughashvili (იოსებ ბესარიონის ძე ჯუღაშვილი), represented in Russian as Iosif Vissarionovich Dzhugashvili (Иосиф Виссарионович Джугашвили; pre-1918: Іосифъ Виссаріоновичъ Джугашвили). He adopted the alias "Stalin" during his revolutionary career, and made it his legal name after the October Revolution.
  8. ^ According to church records, Stalin was born on 18 December [O.S. 6 December] 1878. This birth date is maintained in all surviving pre-Revolution documents, and as late as 1921, Stalin himself listed his birthday as 18 December 1878. After coming to power, Stalin gave his birth date as 21 December [O.S. 9 December] 1879. This became the day his birthday was celebrated in the Soviet Union.[2]
